background.title: Substituting into a formula
background.html:
A formula is a rule written with letters. To substitute means to replace each letter with its number, then work it out.

Example: un = u1 + (n − 1)d with u1 = 36, n = 13 and d = −6.

  • Write it out with brackets: 36 + (13 − 1) × (−6)
  • Brackets first: 13 − 1 = 12
  • Then multiply: 12 × (−6) = −72
  • Then add: 36 + (−72) = −36

The same works for an expression such as 6n − 2: with n = 4 it is 24 − 2 = 22.

The order is always: brackets, then powers, then × and ÷, then + and −. Put negative numbers in brackets so the minus sign is not lost. The small letter in un is not a power: it just says which position the number is in.

background.title: Powers (indices): what 2<sup>5</sup>, (−2)<sup>6</sup> and 2<sup>−1</sup> mean
background.html:
The small raised number says how many times to multiply: 25 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32, the product of five 2s.

  • A negative number to an even power is positive: (−2)6 = 64. To an odd power it stays negative: (−2)3 = −8.
  • Anything (except 0) to the power 0 is 1.
  • A negative power means 1 divided by: 2−1 = 1/2 and 2−3 = 1/8.
  • A fraction power means a root: 91/2 = √9 = 3 and 81/3 = 2, because 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

Going backwards: if r3 = 8 then r = 2. If r2 = 3 then r = √3 or r = −√3, because a negative number squared is also positive. On the calculator use the ^ key: 1.03^10 ≈ 1.344.

background.title: Solving equations, and a pair of equations together
background.html:
Solving means finding the value of the letter. Do the same thing to both sides until the letter is alone: 36 + 4d = 12, take 36 from both sides: 4d = −24, divide both sides by 4: d = −6.

Sometimes you have two equations with the same two letters (called simultaneous equations). If both have exactly one u1, subtract one equation from the other and u1 disappears:

u1 + 12d = 8
u1 + 9d = 14
subtract: 3d = −6, so d = −2

Then put d = −2 back into either equation: u1 = 14 − 9 × (−2) = 32. For geometric sequences you divide one equation by the other instead: u1r4 ÷ u1r = r3.

background.title: Percentages as multipliers
background.html:
A percentage is a number out of 100: 3% = 0.03. So 3% of $5000 is 0.03 × 5000 = $150.

To increase or decrease by a percentage in one step, multiply by one number:

increase by 3%100% + 3% = 103%× 1.03
decrease by 15%100% − 15% = 85%× 0.85
decrease by 20%100% − 20% = 80%× 0.8

Doing it again each year means multiplying again: 3 years at 3% is × 1.03 × 1.03 × 1.03 = × 1.033. Two falls of 10% is × 0.92 = × 0.81, a 19% fall, not 20%, because the second 10% is taken from the smaller value. This is how a salary that rises by 3% a year is worked out, and why money that grows by a percentage is a geometric sequence.

background.title: Fractions: dividing by a fraction, and adding fractions
background.html:
The sum to infinity formula often gives a fraction divided by a fraction.

  • Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by it upside down: 12 ÷ 1/3 = 12 × 3 = 36.
  • Take a fraction from 1 by writing 1 as a fraction: 1 − 2/3 = 3/3 − 2/3 = 1/3.
  • To add fractions, give them the same bottom number first: 1/4 + 1/12 = 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12 = 1/3.

Putting it together: (7/12) ÷ (1 − 7/8) = 7/12 ÷ 1/8 = 7/12 × 8 = 56/12 = 14/3. Paper 1 has no calculator, so practise these by hand.

background.title: Rounding: decimal places and significant figures
background.html:
Decimal places (d.p.) count digits after the decimal point. Significant figures (s.f.) count digits from the first one that is not zero.

5796.3703…2 d.p.5796.37
5796.3703…nearest dollar5796
5796.3703…3 s.f.5800

IB rule: unless the question says otherwise, give answers exactly or correct to 3 significant figures. Money questions usually ask for 2 d.p. or the nearest dollar: read the question and do what it says.

Keep the full calculator value until the very last line. Rounding in the middle of a calculation changes the final answer and can lose the answer mark.

background.title: What a proof is, and why it uses letters
background.html:
Trying examples (2 + 3 = 5, 4 + 5 = 9) only shows a statement works for the numbers you tried. There are infinitely many integers to try. A proof uses letters that stand for any integer, so one argument covers every case.

  • Any even integer can be written 2k, and any odd integer 2k + 1, where k is an integer.
  • Expanding a squared bracket: (x − 3)2 = (x − 3)(x − 3) = x2 − 3x − 3x + 9 = x2 − 6x + 9. It is not x2 + 9.
  • Command words: state means give the answer, no working needed; show that means the answer is already given and the marks are for the steps.
  • Each line must follow from the line before by correct algebra, and the last line says in words why the statement is true.

terms.def: A list of numbers in a set order, usually made by a rule. Example: 2, 5, 8, 11, … (add 3 each time).
The total you get when you add up the numbers of a sequence. 2, 5, 8 is a sequence; 2 + 5 + 8 is a series.
A sequence where you add the same number each time to get the next one. Example: 7, 11, 15, 19 (add 4). Growing arithmetically means growing by the same amount each time.
A sequence where you multiply by the same number each time to get the next one. Example: 2, 4, 8, 16 (multiply by 2).
Going on for ever, with no last one. An infinite sequence never ends.
Having an end or a fixed size; the opposite of infinite. A finite total is an ordinary number, like 50.
∞ is the symbol for infinity, meaning 'for ever'. The sum to infinity, S∞, is the total of all the terms of a geometric sequence that never ends. It only exists when the terms shrink towards 0.
The examiners' answer sheet. It shows the correct answers and which steps of working earn marks.
A booklet of formulas the IB gives you in the exam. This page marks those formulas 'In booklet'; the others you must learn.
A rule written with letters that tells you how to work out a value. Example: u<sub>n</sub> = u<sub>1</sub> + (n − 1)d.
Graphic display calculator: the graphing calculator allowed in Paper 2. It can draw graphs, make tables of values and solve equations for you.
Σ is the Greek capital letter sigma. In maths it means 'add up'. The number below it says where the counting starts, the number on top where it stops.
A whole number above zero: 1, 2, 3, 4, … A position in a sequence is always one of these.
A whole number: positive, negative or zero. Examples: −3, 0, 7. 2.5 is not an integer.
Coming one straight after another, with no gaps. 4, 5, 6 are consecutive integers; u<sub>2</sub> and u<sub>3</sub> are consecutive terms.
Staying the same; not changing.
In an arithmetic sequence, the fixed amount added each time, called d. In 7, 11, 15 it is 4. In 60, 57.5, 55 it is −2.5.
In a geometric sequence, the fixed number you multiply by each time, called r. In 3, 6, 12 it is 2. Find it by dividing a term by the one before.
What you get when you divide one number by another. It says how many times bigger (or smaller) the first is: the ratio of 12 to 3 is 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Here it usually means the common ratio r.
A piece of maths made of numbers and letters joined by +, −, × or ÷, with no = sign. Example: 6n − 2.
A letter that stands for a number that can change, like x, m or n.
The small raised number that says how many times to multiply: in 2<sup>5</sup> = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32 the power is 5. It is also called an index or exponent. An even power is 2, 4, 6, …

Going back from a power. 3 and −3 are the square roots of 9, because 3 × 3 = 9 and (−3) × (−3) = 9. The sign √ means only the positive one: √9 = 3. If r<sup>3</sup> = 8, r is the cube root of 8, which is 2.
A way to find an unknown power. log<sub>2</sub> 8 = 3 because 2<sup>3</sup> = 8. Your class meets it properly in Topic 2; today the GDC can do the same job.
In maths: work out the value. 'Evaluate the sum' means find the single number it equals. (In other IB subjects 'evaluate' means weigh up the good and bad points.)
IB command term: give the answer or a short fact. No working or explanation is needed.
IB command term: get to the result you are given, with every step written. The answer is already on the paper, so all the marks are for the working.
A proof is a chain of correct steps that shows a statement is true in every possible case, not just in some examples. To prove is to write one.
Going step by step from things you know are true to a result that must then also be true.
A sentence in maths that is either true or false, such as 'the sum of two odd numbers is even'.
An equation that is true for every value of the letter, written with ≡. Example: (x + 1)2 ≡ x2 + 2x + 1 for any x you choose.
Left-hand side: everything to the left of the = or ≡ sign.
Right-hand side: everything to the right of the = or ≡ sign.
Multiply out the brackets. Example: 3(x + 2) becomes 3x + 6.
The opposite of expand: take out a number or letter that divides every part, and put the rest in brackets. Example: 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1).

One bottom number shared by fractions, so they can be added. For <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> + <sup>1</sup>/<sub>12</sub> use twelfths: <sup>3</sup>/<sub>12</sub> + <sup>1</sup>/<sub>12</sub> = <sup>4</sup>/<sub>12</sub>.
The bottom number of a fraction. In <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub> it is 4. A denominator can never be zero.

Remove something that is both on the top and the bottom of a fraction, because it divides to 1. Example: <sup>2 × 5</sup>/<sub>2 × 7</sub> = <sup>5</sup>/<sub>7</sub>. 'Cancel exactly' can also mean positive and negative numbers add to 0.
Add together the parts of an expression that are alike: 9 + 5 = 14, and 2x + 3x = 5x.
Rewrite x<sup>2</sup> + bx + c as (x + p)<sup>2</sup> + q. It helps because a square, (x + p)<sup>2</sup>, can never be negative.
Divisible by 3 means it divides by 3 exactly, with nothing left over. 15 is divisible by 3; 16 is not.
An integer times itself: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, … (1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3, …).
The answer when you multiply. The product of 3 and 5 is 15.
The size of a number without its sign, written with two straight lines. |−2| = 2 and |2| = 2. |r| < 1 means r is between −1 and 1.
A series converges when its running total gets closer and closer to one fixed number, so the sum to infinity exists.
'Is approximately equal to': close to, but rounded.
'Plus or minus': both answers are possible. r = ±√3 means r = √3 or r = −√3.
'Is not equal to'. r ≠ 0 means r cannot be 0.
'Is greater than or equal to'. ≤ means 'is less than or equal to'. Without the line, > and < mean greater than and less than.
Money a bank pays you for keeping your money there (or you pay for borrowing). It is usually a percentage per year.
Interest worked out on the starting amount only, so you get the same amount every year. The total grows like an arithmetic sequence.
Interest that is added to the money in the account, so next time you also earn interest on the interest. The total grows like a geometric sequence.
'Compounded monthly' means the interest is worked out and added to the account every month. A compounding period is the time between two such additions.

The figure as stated, before anything is changed or taken off. A nominal 5% a year compounded monthly means <sup>5</sup>/<sub>12</sub>% each month. A nominal value is the amount of money before removing the effect of inflation.
When something loses value over time, like a car that is worth less each year. Losing 15% a year means multiplying by 0.85 each year.
Put money somewhere, such as a bank account, so that it grows. The money put in is the investment.
Yearly; once a year. Compounded annually means interest is added once a year.
Quarterly: four times a year, every 3 months. Half-yearly: twice a year, every 6 months.
The amount of money in an account at a given time.
The fixed amount a person is paid for their job, usually given per year.
Buying something. '10 years after purchase' means 10 years after it was bought.

A program on the GDC for money questions. You enter what you know and it finds the missing value. N = years, I% = yearly rate, PMT = regular payment (0 here), P/Y and C/Y = payments and compounding periods per year.
A GDC tool: you type in an equation and it finds the value of the unknown letter.
The digits after the decimal point. 5.2403 to two decimal places is 5.24.
Close to the true value but not exact. To approximate is to find such a value, for example by rounding or averaging.
A formula that describes a real situation well enough to make predictions, even if it does not fit perfectly.
Predicting a value outside the range of the numbers you have, such as week 10 when you only know weeks 1 to 5. It is less reliable than predicting inside that range.
Likely to be correct, so you can trust it.
The same on both sides of a middle point. 36, 30, …, −30, −36 is symmetric about 0: each number has a partner with the opposite sign.
Switch back and forth every time: +, −, +, −, …
Work out a formula yourself, step by step, from things you already know.
Give a correct reason why a step is allowed.
Treat something as true without having shown it is true.
The last line of a proof: a sentence that says what you have shown and why it is true.
Correct and acceptable. A valid proof really does prove the statement for every case.
Goes above; is more than.
The symbols and way of writing that maths uses, such as u<sub>n</sub> for a term or Σ for 'add up'.
Maths with letters that stand for numbers. An algebraic proof uses letters, so it covers every number; a numerical one uses actual numbers.
A rule that must be true. 'The condition |r| < 1' means the sum to infinity only exists when r is between −1 and 1.
Prices going up over time, so the same money buys less. 2% inflation means things cost 2% more each year.
What an amount of money is worth in today's prices, after taking off the effect of inflation.
IB command term: get a number as the answer, and show the steps of working that lead to it.
IB command term: describe the differences between two things, talking about both of them.
Break something down into its parts to see how it works. Here: look closely at the numbers to find the pattern.
IB command term: use what you know to spot patterns and say what the results mean in the real situation.
IB command term: give a short judgement about a result, for example whether it is sensible or how far you can trust it.
Not linked to each other. Two independent letters, a and b, can each be any integer, so the two numbers can be different.
IB command term: get the answer and show the steps of working that lead to it. A bare answer may not get all the marks.
IB command term: say what result you expect, for example a value for week 10 worked out from the pattern so far.
